#0 Summary: the key insights, implications and conclusions

The decision for Richard: will the market pay the ten-year median multiple of 9.3x for a delivering Rexel, or only the guideline's 8.38x?
+2.9%
total return to December 2027 at the guideline multiple of 8.38x: the de-rating cancels the earnings growth
about +13%
total return to December 2027 at the 9.3x median, my central case, on the same earnings

The business. Rexel is the world's second- or third-largest distributor of electrical products to professional customers, with €19.4bn of sales in 2025 (Europe 48%, North America 46%, Asia-Pacific 6%). Rexel earns a thin spread, an EBITA margin of about 6-7% on a 25% gross margin, on a very large flow of other companies' products. Rexel's profit therefore moves far more with price and mix than with volume: product inflation on a fixed branch base lifted the margin from 5.0% to 7.3% in 2019-22, and deflation plus a European construction slump took it back to 5.9% in 2024.

Rexel leads or co-leads its core European markets (France is close to a duopoly with Sonepar), is a mid-sized challenger in the fragmented US market, and has the best working-capital discipline in the sector (14-15% of sales, against about 20% at Wesco).

The investment case. Rexel's earnings are compounding at about 12% a year to 2028 on four identifiable drivers.

Price and copperLargely delivered in 2026.
US data centres13% of US sales, with growth decelerating from triple digits.
The $1.4bn GCG acquisitionConsolidated mechanically from January 2027; adds about 22bp to the group margin.
Self-helpRecord productivity of 4%, turnarounds in the UK and Germany, and AI tools.

Guidance has been raised twice in 2026 from a deliberately conservative base, and it is still a floor. Viewforth's EBITA forecasts sit 3-4% above a consensus that predates most of the revisions made after the Q3 release.

Yet the shares have decoupled from their peers. Over six months Rexel fell 4.7% while the European distributor basket rose 20.7%, and 84% of the variance in Rexel's share price is now specific to the company. The market is pricing three concerns rather than the operating delivery: France (a spread of 174bp between French and German ten-year government bond yields, an election in April-May 2027 and a corporate tax surcharge now being extended); the €500m share placing at €34.75 (4.6% dilution, buybacks paused, leverage of 2.3x pro forma, a BB+ credit rating); and an indirect, second-order exposure to AI spending through customers' data centres.

The central tension decides the return: Rexel is cheap against its peers and not cheap against its own history. The two-year-forward P/E expanded from 7-8x in 2022-24 to 13.0x in February 2026 on trough earnings. Since February the multiple has deflated through earnings growth rather than through the share price: the price is roughly where it was in February, while the multiple is two turns lower.

Rexel is cheap against its peers but dear against its own history, and the gap between the two decides the return.

The dashboard reads Rexel's phase as Bottoming, and its guideline fair multiple for that phase is 8.38x, the 30th percentile of the ten-year range. At 8.38x, the model's total return is +2.9% to December 2027 (earnings +17.6%, multiple -19.1%, dividends +7.8%) and +18.9% to June 2029 (+6.7% a year). The return is therefore almost entirely a judgement about where the multiple settles: at the 18-month point, each turn of forward P/E is worth about €3.70 a share, 11% of today's price.

Where the skew is unusually positive, and where it is not.

  • Positive: operating upgrades over the next six to twelve months. FY2026 guidance (same-day sales growth of about 7% and a margin of at least 6.4%) will be met or beaten with about 90% probability; Viewforth expects 7.25% and 6.50%. The first FY2027 outlook, on 10 February 2027, will be set below Viewforth's base case (I expect "3-5%" growth and a margin of "around 6.7%", against Viewforth's 4.5% and 6.80%), which makes a raise in July 2027 the single most likely guidance event (about 50%). Consensus EBITA should rise 3-5% for 2026 and 4-8% for 2027 as brokers absorb the Q3 beat and consolidate GCG, which nine of thirteen brokers still exclude.
  • Not positive: the EPS line in February 2027. Consensus 2027 EPS of €3.00 assumes that the French tax surcharge lapses (a 27% tax rate, where Viewforth carries 29%), uses a share count 1-5% too low and, in several models, omits GCG's interest cost and PPA. The operating beat will therefore arrive with a below-the-line reset of consensus EPS of about -3% to -8%, a headline driven by tax, share count and accounting rather than by the franchise. Sophisticated holders will look through the reset; the share price may not on the day.
  • The real risk is correlated, not cyclical. Copper ($14,000/t, against the guidance assumption of $11,000/t), hyperscaler capex and GCG's engineered products all depend on the same AI-and-electrification trade. A financing crack in AI capex that also knocked copper would remove 30-45bp of margin and 2-3 points of growth within two quarters, because deflation drops through at 35-40bp of margin per point of organic decline, against only 5-7bp per point on the way up.

Phase and fair multiple: my view against the guideline. Two clocks are running. The fundamentals are in a reinforcing phase: six quarters of sequential improvement, volume growth in every region, a 3.4-month backlog, two guidance raises and an acquisition that shifts the mix. The share price stalled in February 2026 and is bottoming on overhangs that are time-limited: the absorption of the placing, the French budget (final vote in December) and GCG's closing (year-end).

The guideline's 8.38x is a trough-phase multiple for a case that is delivering. The ten-year median of 9.3x is reachable within 18 months if the February results beat and the French budget passes without an enlarged surcharge; at 9.3x, the model's +3% return becomes about +13% to December 2027 and +31% to June 2029. I would not underwrite a return toward 12x: for a BB+-rated, French-listed, copper-exposed distributor, a two-year-forward P/E above 11x has only ever occurred at points of trough earnings.

Read together, the five judgements show that the multiple matters most. Each operating judgement (1-3) moves EPS by 3-9%, while the multiple judgement moves the price by 11% a turn. That is why this memo spends as much effort on the phase, the fair multiple and the return (#10-#12) as on the operations. The FY2027 EPS range runs from about €2.42 (bear case, 20% probability) to €3.36 (bull case, 25%) around a base of €2.97 (55%). The range is skewed down on EPS and flat on FCF, which is €700-780m in every scenario because working capital releases cash when copper or volume fall.

#1 Tailwinds in the operating environment, and the absence of headwinds

Evidence. Rexel's operating environment turned from headwind to tailwind over 2025-26, and Q3 2026 was Rexel's strongest quarter since 2022.

Q3 2026 was the strongest quarter since 2022, with growth in every region and volume, not only price, behind it.

+11.4%
group same-day sales: volume +6.3%, cable price +2.9%, non-cable price +2.2%
+17.4%
North America
+4.5%
Europe
+15.8%
Asia-Pacific

Four external forces are pushing Rexel's growth.

  • The data-centre power build-out. US data centres rose from about 5% of Rexel's US sales in late 2025 to 13% in Q3 2026, on triple-digit growth. Data centres make up a quarter of a North American backlog of more than $3bn (3.4 months of sales, up from 2.7 months in December 2025); no project has been delayed or cancelled, and management sees "no signs of pre-buying". Rexel captures less of the build-out than Wesco, where data centres are 23% of sales and about four times Rexel's data-centre revenue, but the wave is large enough that even a small share makes data centres Rexel's biggest volume driver.
  • Product inflation. Copper trades above $14,000/t, against guidance built on $11,000/t; Schneider raised prices 5.5% and Legrand 3.6% in Q3; and the US Section 232 and 301 tariffs create a price umbrella that Rexel passes through. Each $1,000/t of copper is worth about 1 point of organic growth and 10-15bp of margin.
  • European electrification and energy security. Energy-transition categories (heating, ventilation and air conditioning; solar; electric-vehicle charging) are 22% of European sales and grew about 13-15%. Brent crude at $111, heat waves and policy help: France's €10bn-a-year electrification plan, Germany's Building Modernisation Act from 2027 and the EU's Energy Performance of Buildings Directive.
  • US industrial automation and vendor consolidation. US industrial automation sales grew 20% in Q3 on reshoring and the Revere acquisition, and customers are consolidating their purchasing onto the three national distributors.

The headwinds are real: core construction is still contracting, and France weighs on the group. Construction indicators in Europe and the US remain in contraction (table below). France, about 20% of sales and a disproportionate share of European profit, brings a sovereign bond spread at its widest since 2011, an election in April-May 2027 and a corporate tax surcharge that keeps the group's tax rate near 29-30%. The US dollar, 38% of sales and unhedged, turned from a 2.6% drag on growth in H1 to a 1.2% tailwind in Q3; with GCG, dollar sales pass half of the group.

Construction indicatorLatest reading
Eurozone construction PMI43.4 (seventh month below 50)
France construction PMI39.8
UK construction starts-29%
US Architecture Billings Index44.7
US mortgage rates7.1-7.3%, with the Federal Reserve still raising rates

Inference. Decomposed, the Q3 tailwind is narrower than the headline but broader than in H1. Price made up 45% of Q3 growth and data centres roughly a quarter. The change since H1 is that US sales outside data centres grew about 11% (about 6% in volume) and European volume turned positive.

The inputs, however, are at or near their peak rate of change. At flat prices, copper's year-on-year gain compresses to zero by mid-2027; data-centre comparisons double; and supplier price rises are at a cyclical high. Growth from these inputs therefore slows in 2027 even if their levels hold.

The replacement driver, European construction, has no supporting indicator yet. Rexel's European volume base is, however, depressed: group volumes are barely above 2019, and revenue is only 3.8% above 2022 despite acquisitions. A European recovery in 2027-28 would therefore add to growth rather than reverse it. That asymmetry between limited further downside and real upside in European volume is the bull case's best foundation.

So what. 2026 is secured, and 2027 is the test. In H1 2027, growth is supported by the backlog and an easy comparison (Q1 2026 grew 3.4%); in H2 2027, growth faces the hardest comparison since 2022 (H2 2026 at about +9.4%). Viewforth's 2027 organic growth of 4.5% (H1 +5.5%, H2 +3.5%) sits below Morgan Stanley (5.8%) and Bernstein (5.3%) and close to a consensus of about 4.7%.

Where I differ from the market. The bulls read Q3 as structural and the bears read it as copper; both are half right. The bears under-weight the breadth of the Q3 volume recovery, and the bulls under-weight the H2 2027 comparison. I agree with the market on two points: European construction will not help in 2027, and France is a genuine drag on the multiple, if not yet on the numbers (French sales grew 3.6% in Q3).

Counter-case and what would change my view. The strongest counter-case is correlation: hyperscaler capex finances the data-centre volume, GCG's demand and part of the copper price, so a financing shock would hit all three. Early signs of such a shock exist: New York's pause on permits for data centres above 50MW, Illinois' suspension of incentives and Deutsche Bank's warning on the credit of neocloud providers. I would turn more cautious if copper stayed below $12,000/t for a quarter or the backlog fell below 2.8 months. I would turn more positive if the Eurozone construction PMI rose back above 47, or if French housing starts (+31% in September, and a lead indicator of Rexel's European growth by about a quarter) held up through the winter.

Conclusion: a moderate, narrowing tailwind that secures 2026 and the first half of 2027, with the headwinds concentrated in the share price (France, rates, risk-off) rather than in the P&L.

Score: 65, set by the Rater. Four real external legs (US data-centre power at 13% of US sales with a 3.4-month backlog, copper and supplier price, European electrification at 22% of European sales, US automation and vendor consolidation) drove Q3 same-day growth of +11.4% with volume positive in every region, but about half is price, the inputs are at their peak rate of change into 2027, and core construction in Europe and the US is still contracting; consensus sales growth at the 44th percentile shows how much of this fades. A clear but partial, narrowing net positive, in line with the External change forces group (60) and a notch above it for the breadth of the Q3 volume recovery.

#2 Internally-driven corporate change forces, and the absence of problems

Evidence. The internal picture is the stronger half of the case, and in the last six months Rexel's internal change moved from aspiration to capital commitment.

  • Guidance raised twice in 2026 (the steps are shown in #4), with the copper assumption left at $11,000/t.
  • The GCG acquisition. GCG costs $1.4bn of enterprise value for more than $1.1bn of revenue at an 11% EBITA margin, with a 13% target, and it is Rexel's largest deal in 15 years. GCG sells 75% proprietary or value-added products, such as cable bus systems that cut installation time by 60% and prefabricated power "whips" that let equipment be powered up ten times faster. The deal directly targets Rexel's diagnosed weakness, its under-exposure to data-centre white space and to utilities: before GCG, data centres were 8% of Rexel's US sales against Wesco's 18%. GCG adds more than 20bp to the group margin from year one, lifts North America above half of sales and moves the portfolio toward the 60/40 core-to-specialty target. The earlier 2026 bolt-ons (Revere, a Rockwell automation partner; DEE; Techno-Contact 360) and the Talley wireless deal point the same way, while Rexel exited Finland, New Zealand and the Middle East.
  • Self-help with numbers (table below). The CEO's commitment to a margin above 7% "between 2027 and 2029, without meaningful volume recovery" is unusual because it is explicitly independent of volume.
  • Governance and ownership. Cevian (23%, a holder since 2016) took a board seat in October 2025 and backed the rejection of QXO's €28-28.40 bid; a former Iberdrola CEO joins as a board observer as Rexel buys a utility-exposed platform. The bonus design (40% gross margin, 40% EBITA margin, 20% working capital) matches the strategy.

The problems are real but contained. The balance sheet paid for the strategy. Rexel raised €500m of equity at €34.75 (4.9% more shares outstanding), paused buybacks (previously €50-150m a year) and has held the dividend at €1.20 since 2022. Leverage was 2.4x at June 2026 and will be about 2.3x pro forma for GCG at year-end. The credit ratings are BB+/Ba1, the top of speculative grade and not investment grade as several broker notes imply; with the covenant at 3.5x, leverage is not a constraint. Because of the placing and the buyback pause, per-share earnings lag group earnings by about four points in 2027.

Management bandwidth is stretched: four acquisitions, two country turnarounds and one leader now covering France, Benelux, Italy and the UK, while succession readiness has slipped to 80%. Insider alignment is thin: the CEO holds less than 0.1% of the shares, insiders made no open-market purchases in 2026, and long-term pay has no ROCE metric, a gap in an acquisitive phase. A €48m judicial guarantee sits behind a €124m antitrust fine under appeal.

Half-yearly revenue growth had only returned to +2.2% by H1 2026, while FactSet's net debt (including leases) rose to about 3x EBITDA ahead of the placing.

Inference. Rexel is a self-improving company riding a sector tailwind, not a company undergoing massive change. Self-help is worth about 15-20bp of margin a year net of wage inflation, enough to lift the floor of the forecast range more than its centre.

GCG's year-one accretion, about +2.5% of EPS before PPA and roughly nil after it, is mostly financial. Two-thirds of the price is funded with debt at about 4%, against an acquired earnings yield of about 8.5-10%. The after-tax return on the €1.2bn invested is about 7% in year one, rising to about 9% by 2029 if GCG reaches its 13% margin, which is around the 9% cost of capital. GCG is a good strategic and mix decision, but at the price paid it does not create value unless synergies exceed plan.

Where I differ from the market. The sell-side quotes GCG's EPS accretion as "3% rising to 8%" without decomposing it; I would present GCG to Richard as a lever for the narrative and the margin rather than for EPS. On the pause in capital returns, the market is if anything too relaxed: 2027 EPS growth of 12% would be about 16% on the old share count with buybacks.

Counter-case and what would change my view. The strongest counter-case is integration risk. GCG is engineering-led, manufactures products and sells into hyperscaler tenders, where Bernstein fears that competitive bidding will dilute the 11-13% margin. US industry experts have criticised Rexel's centralised operating model, and Rexel's own 2018 restructuring cost 16% of German sales and 6% of UK sales.

Three readings would change my view. GCG's first consolidated half (reported in July 2027) at or above an 11% margin, with standalone growth above 8%, would move me toward Bernstein's 7.2% group margin for 2027; a quantified synergy plan and segment disclosure in February would also help. A dividend increase for FY2026 would be a small but telling signal of confidence: Viewforth holds the dividend at €1.20, and the flat record since 2022 and the priority given to the balance sheet make an increase a coin toss.

Conclusion: strong, broad and well-articulated internal change, resourced at the temporary cost of per-share capital returns, whose earnings effect is front-loaded into 2026-27 and whose execution test is GCG in H1 2027.

Score: 71, set by the Rater. A funded, multi-part programme: the $1.4bn GCG acquisition (largest in 15 years, aimed at the diagnosed data-centre and utility weakness, about +22bp of group margin), record 4% productivity, UK and Germany margins up more than 100bp, AI and digital cost-to-serve and portfolio pruning, under a CEO who commits to a volume-independent margin above 7%; netted for the 4.9% dilution, paused buybacks, stretched bandwidth and GCG returns only around the cost of capital, which make per-share earnings lag group earnings by about four points. I sit above the Internal change forces group (64) because a move of GCG's size is a large change force in itself, but below Instalco's proven turnaround.

#3 Industry structure, competitive advantage, financial profile, management

Industry and value chain. The structure of electrical distribution is moderately supportive of Rexel and fairly robust, but it caps Rexel's margin in the middle of the value chain.

What supports the structure

  • Concentrated European national markets support price discipline: Rexel has more than 30% share in France, Benelux, Austria and Sweden, and France is effectively a duopoly.
  • The fragmented US market (top five about one-third; more than 5,000 operators) gives a long acquisition runway at about 6x EBITDA.
  • The large competitors (Sonepar, private and the largest at €33.6bn; Wesco; Graybar) put margin first.
  • Suppliers set branded product prices, which rarely fall (Legrand has not cut its average prices in twenty years), so the industry does not start price wars when volume declines, except in commodity categories (cable, solar, PVC) that deflate hard.
  • Capital intensity is low: capex is about 1% of sales.

What limits it

  • Rexel sits in the low-margin middle of a chain in which the original equipment manufacturers earn 18-25% EBIT margins and hold specification power.
  • Hyperscalers buy transformers and switchgear directly from manufacturers, leaving distributors 35-40% of a data centre's electrical bill of materials.

Competitive advantage. Rexel's advantage is real but moderate, and it rests on cost and availability rather than on pricing power. Its sources are branch and hub density where Rexel leads (1,876 branches, 64 hubs and fill rates of 92-95%; customers rank availability and delivery far above digital ordering); purchasing scale (more than $20bn a year, half of it from 28 suppliers); a capability to serve national accounts that only Sonepar and Wesco share; a lead in digital and data that is narrowing against Sonepar but widening against independents; and sector-best working capital.

Rexel's gross margin has held in a 24.9-25.5% band through inflation and deflation, which shows that Rexel passes prices through rather than keeping them. GCG adds an emerging layer of engineered value-add, where labour-saving products support value pricing. Net: Rexel's moat supports a through-cycle margin of 6-7.5%, not a premium margin.

About four-fifths of revenue goes through the warehouse and branch network, the base of Rexel's cost-and-availability advantage.

Financial profile. Rexel's financial profile is above average for a distributor on cash and working capital, average on returns and below average on margin. Post-tax returns on tangible capital are about 18%, but ROCE is about 10% because Rexel buys much of its growth. FCF conversion has been above 65% of EBITDA after leases for three years, including the year of the antitrust fine. EPS is cyclical, moving about ±25-35% across a cycle, but the trough margin has risen about 200bp over two cycles (5.9% in 2024, against about 4% in older troughs).

Against its peers, Rexel matches Legrand and Beijer Ref on consensus EPS growth but earns half their margin or less and converts less of its profit to cash (table below). The same margin gap is also why Rexel has the most room to improve.

Management is a clear strength. Guillaume Texier (CEO since 2021, renewed to 2029) previously took Saint-Gobain's Southern Europe, Middle East and Africa region from a 4.6% to an 8.3% margin. At Rexel he defended a 6% margin through a deep European downturn, cut costs fast, cut guidance once and honestly (October 2024) and then delivered the cut guidance to the decimal, and executed the largest deal in 15 years on disciplined post-synergy terms. The CFO has been in place since 2017.

For a modeller, Rexel's disclosure is among the best in its peer group: growth split into volume, cable price and non-cable price; the copper assumption; a half-year margin bridge; the delta-inflation line (selling-price inflation less opex inflation); and the backlog in months. Rexel's goals are stretching for Rexel but moderate against peers (the Axelerate 2028 plan: sales growth of 5-8%, a margin above 7% and digital sales at 50%), and the ambition is rising with GCG. The culture is congruent with the strategy, if not at the level of system design seen at Lifco or Ryanair.

Where I differ from the market. The market frames Rexel as a lower-quality Wesco. I agree on the margin level and on white space, where management itself says it cannot match Wesco's margins. I weight more heavily than the market two strengths that Wesco does not have: a working-capital model about five points of sales leaner, and a guidance style that has become a reliable floor. The market also under-rates how much the 200bp-higher trough margin matters for the multiple that a cyclical deserves.

Counter-case and what would change my view. Rexel's three-year revenue growth of 2.2% a year trails Wesco (8.6%), Graybar (8.0%) and Sonepar (6.0%): Rexel was the least advantaged of the global distributors in the 2022-25 cycle. If the next cycle again rewards data-centre exposure over cost and digital efficiency, that ranking persists. I would upgrade my view of the foundations if GCG proves that Rexel can run an engineered business at a 13% margin and if the UK and Germany reach the European average margin (about 6%) by 2028, which I put at about 40% probability.

Conclusion: a well-run, capital-light, cash-generative operator with real but moderate advantages in a rational industry, whose financial profile is average for European industrials and whose management is better than its margin.

Score: 52, set by the Rater. Qualitatively a leading position in a margin-capped structure: near-duopoly European cores, rational margin-first rivals, low capital intensity and a capable, transparent management (group 65), but a cost-and-availability moat with pricing borrowed from suppliers in the low-margin middle of the chain (groups 56 and 50). The figures agree (ROIC 6.3%, 47th percentile; EBITDA margin 12th percentile; EPS down 13% a year over three years), and new capital (GCG) earns about 7-9% against a 9% cost of capital, while EPS swings 25-35% across a cycle; the 200bp higher trough margin and sector-best working capital keep it just above the middle, close to the Asker Healthcare and Munters level.

#4 Conservative guidance, expectation management and the delivery record

Evidence. Rexel is the archetype of precise sandbagging. Management sets a beatable floor on conservative inputs, raises the floor in small steps as visibility improves ("around" becomes "at least"; 3-5% becomes about 5%, then about 7%), delivers at or slightly above the top of the range, and cuts quickly when conditions turn. The record is in the table below; in 2026, guidance was confirmed in April despite a Q1 miss and then raised in July and October.

Rexel sets a beatable floor and raises it in small steps: 2026 has been raised twice, and the first FY2027 guide should again start below our base.

Current FY2026 guidance still implies Q4 same-day growth of only about 6%, after 7.3% over nine months and 11.4% in Q3, with the backlog up 0.7 months and copper 40% above a year earlier. Viewforth's 7.25% growth and 6.50% margin are therefore a small beat, not a heroic one. Against consensus, the pattern is beats on margin and occasional misses on volume: Q1 2026 missed on weather, and Q2 and Q3 beat by 1.3 and 4.8 points.

Sell-side management. Rexel's guidance sat below consensus at every point in 2026: the February guide of 3-5% growth compared with a consensus of 5.6%. Management's informal commentary is confident on self-help ("6% has become what we deliver") and cautious on volume ("prudence on construction"; US sales outside data centres were described as "slightly negative" until they were not). The mid-term target was re-dated, not raised. In October management pointedly declined to guide on 2027 while flagging tougher data-centre comparisons, fluctuating European subsidies and lower gross margins on large projects: the language of a company preparing a cautious guide.

Inference. I expect the first FY2027 outlook, on 10 February 2027, to be "low-to-mid single digit" or 3-5% same-day growth and a margin of "around 6.7%" including GCG, with the copper assumption raised only modestly. That outlook would be about 1 point of growth and 10-20bp of margin below Viewforth's base case, and 1-2 points and 40-50bp below Bernstein. A beatable floor is good for the share price over twelve months, but it carries a risk on the day of release, because investors have been reading Jefferies ("positive guidance framework") and Bernstein (a 7.2% margin).

Where I differ from the market. The three most bullish brokers treat guidance conservatism as a given; the two Holds and the Sell (Barclays: target €30, 2027 EPS €2.80) argue that the self-help is already in the price. I side with the bulls on direction, and I add one point that the market has not priced: the February headline will pair an operating beat with a reset of the EPS basis (a tax rate of about 30% if the surcharge is extended, a first PPA estimate for GCG and the full post-placing share count), which most of consensus has not modelled.

Counter-case and what would change my view. Rexel's one honest cut (October 2024) came from solar and PVC deflation plus European construction, and it arrived within two quarters of a confident H1. A copper price below about $11,500/t or a backlog below 2.8 months would make a cut in October 2027 (about 15% probability today) the base case rather than the tail.

Conclusion: guidance is deliberately below our forecasts at every horizon and has been beaten in every upswing year, so the probability of raises over the next twelve months (about 50% for FY2027, most likely in July) is well above the European average.

Score: 76, set by the Rater. A deliberate beatable-floor style: 2023 met, 2025 beaten on growth and cash, 2026 raised twice from a guide set below consensus, and current FY2026 guidance implies only about 6% Q4 growth after a Q3 at 11.4%, so it is still a floor; management is visibly preparing a cautious FY2027 guide. Held below Ithaca and Nexans by the October 2024 cut inside the window (met exactly afterwards) and occasional volume misses against consensus, consistent with the Guidance group (72).

#5 The business model's leverage: pricing, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost-out and feedback loops

The mechanics, measured. Rexel's gross margin is about 25%, and its opex, including depreciation, is about 19% of sales (€3.7bn), of which 72% is fixed and 68% is personnel and delivery. In theory, price is Rexel's stronger lever (tiles below): 1% of price at a constant gross-margin percentage adds more EBITA than 1% of volume, at no extra cost. Rexel needs about 2% of price or 2.5% of productivity a year just to offset opex inflation.

A fixed cost base makes price the most powerful lever: 1% of price adds more EBITA than 1% of volume, at no extra cost.

In practice, the slope is asymmetric (chart below). On the way up, the margin gains only 5-7bp per point of organic growth, because inflation and investment absorb part of the gain. On the way down, the margin loses 15-25bp per point for volume alone and 35-40bp per point when price falls with volume. Financial leverage multiplies the effect by about 1.2x (net financial items are about 18% of EBITA in 2027), so a 10% move in EBITA is about a 12% move in EPS.

Pricing power. Rexel's pricing power is borrowed, not owned. Rexel passes supplier and copper inflation through promptly and in full (selling prices rose 5.1% in Q3), which lifts gross profit in euros on a fixed cost base. Rexel does not, however, widen its own spread: selling-price inflation less opex inflation was -19bp in 2025 and only +6bp in H1 2026, and non-cable price rises (1.1-2.2%) run below suppliers' list-price rises (2-5.5%).

Genuine pricing power exists in GCG's engineered products, which save customers 20-60% of installation labour, and in AI-assisted quoting. Together these are only about 6-8% of sales after GCG, too small to change the group spread before 2029. In 2027 the spread turns slightly negative again (-7bp in Viewforth's margin bridge), as copper stops rising and non-cable price of about 1.7% meets opex inflation of about 2.6%.

Cost-out. About 5-10% of opex (€190-370m gross) can be removed over three years through AI in customer service and inside sales (12,000 staff; 10-15% productivity claimed), logistics automation (from 10 to 20 automated centres) and branch rationalisation in the UK and Germany. Most of that saving is spent offsetting wage inflation: what reaches the margin is about 15-20bp a year to 2028 and about 10bp a year thereafter. Viewforth assumes that competition takes back half of the AI saving from 2028, because 39% of distributors in Morgan Stanley's Q3 survey report no measurable AI gain and rivals buy the same tools. The purpose of cost-out at Rexel is insulation: cost-out raised the trough margin from about 4% in past downturns to about 6% in 2024.

Feedback loops. Four reinforcing loops carry the margin up and four balancing loops pull it back (diagram below). The largest balancing loop, the mean reversion of copper and supplier prices, explains most of the slowdown in organic growth from about 7% in 2026 to about 4.5% in 2027. The working-capital loop is the most useful fact for predictability: working capital absorbs cash in inflationary upswings and releases it in downturns, so Rexel's FCF is countercyclical and steadier than its EPS.

Reinforcing loops carry the margin up, while the largest balancing loop, copper and supplier price reverting, explains most of 2027's slowdown.

Reinforcing

  • GCG's mix and specialty pivot: strongest once closed
  • Digital and AI cost-to-serve: moderate, time-limited
  • Vendor consolidation onto scale distributors: durable, volume more than margin
  • Bolt-ons at 6x: strong historically, switched off until 2028

Balancing

  • Copper and supplier-price mean reversion: the largest
  • Wage inflation against productivity
  • Data-centre growth against gross margin and tender intensity
  • Working capital: absorbs cash in upswings, releases it in downturns, so FCF is countercyclical

So what for the forecasts. Revenue growth turns into outsized profit growth when price is the driver (2021: +196bp of margin on 15.6% revenue growth), and into only modest profit growth when volume is the driver. The model's 2027 EBITA growth of 15% on revenue growth of 10.5% comes mostly from GCG's mix (+22bp of margin) and volume leverage (+20bp), with the price spread, digital investment and project dilution taking back about 22bp. The 2027 margin range is about 6.15-7.15% around 6.80%.

Where I differ from the market. Broker sensitivities treat Rexel's operating leverage as symmetrical; the history says the downside slope is three to four times the upside slope. That asymmetry is the single most important fact to carry into the risk and multiple judgements: a cheap cyclical with asymmetric leverage deserves a prudent multiple, not a peak one.

Counter-case and what would change my view. Bernstein notes that data-centre project profitability is "approaching regional margin levels", so the fear of gross-margin dilution is fading; and supplier list prices are still rising, which could hold the price spread positive into H1 2027 (worth about +10bp). A delta-inflation reading above +10bp at the H1 2027 results, or a Q4 margin drop-through above 7bp per point of growth, would move me toward the top of the margin range.

Conclusion: the model turns revenue growth into profit growth powerfully when price leads and modestly when volume leads, with a downside slope three to four times the upside; 2027's profit growth is bought (GCG) and self-made more than it is operationally geared.

Score: 62, set by the Rater. Real structural operating gearing: 72% of opex is fixed, so 1% of volume adds about 3% to EBITA and 1% of price about 4%, proven both ways (+230bp of margin in 2019-22, -90bp in 2024), with cost-out of 15-20bp a year and financial leverage adding about 1.2x; but the pricing power is borrowed (price-over-opex spread -19bp in 2025, about -7bp in 2027), the up-slope is only 5-7bp per point against 15-40bp on the way down, and the forecast EPS-to-revenue growth ratio of about 1.9x is the Universe's median. Large leverage in the structure that disappoints on the way up, so the upper part of the 50 level, above the Economic strength group (45).

Where the growth comes from. The increase in EBITA of about €510m from 2025 to 2028 splits roughly half and half between revenue growth at the old 6.0% margin (about €270m, of which GCG and bolt-ons contribute about €90m) and the 100bp margin step (about €240m).

The margin step itself is spread across several levers (chart below). Price and copper, which drove almost all of the margin gain in 2019-22, contribute only about 15% of this cycle's increase; GCG contributes about a third and self-help about a quarter. The forecast is therefore less dependent on inflation than the last up-cycle and more dependent on execution, and it rests on two items with no history inside Rexel: GCG and hyperscale data centres.

Scope for double-digit growth and for more than the past. EPS compounds at about 12% a year from 2025 to 2030 (about 13% a year to 2028), against about 11% a year over 2019-25 from a trough base. EPS passes the 2022 peak (€3.09) in 2028 and exceeds it by 30% in 2030. The margin averages about 7.0% over 2027-30, against about 6.0% over 2019-25, and by 2030 it reaches a level previously seen only in the 2022 inflation spike, this time without inflation.

Revenue growth after 2027 (4-4.5% a year) is below the Axelerate range of 5-8%, because bolt-on acquisitions stay below 2-3% of revenue a year until leverage allows more. The base case excludes about €0.5-0.8bn of acquisition capacity that becomes available with leverage below 2x by 2029. FCF per share roughly doubles, from about €1.55 in 2025 to about €3.05 in 2028, a 9% yield on today's price, and leverage is back below 2x from end-2027 in every scenario except the bear case.

Over FY2019-25 earnings recovered from a trough but in 2025 were still below the 2022 peak, which the forecasts pass in 2028.

Where I differ from the market. Viewforth is above consensus on margin in every year (6.50% against 6.30% for 2026; 6.80% against 6.59% for 2027; 7.00% against 6.90% for 2028), because GCG's mix effect is mechanical and Rexel's margin record is good. Viewforth is below the most bullish brokers (Bernstein: 7.2% in 2027 and 7.6% in 2028), because peers retain less of their productivity gains than they announce. On 2027 EPS, Viewforth is 8% below consensus on a like-for-like basis, for reasons of policy and accounting rather than operations.

Consensus EPS rises from €2.53 for FY2026 to €3.31 for FY2028 on the brokers' basis, the line on which our like-for-like 2027 EPS sits about 8% lower.

Counter-case and what would change my view. The earlier research sets and the brokers were all too conservative on the 2026 run-rate (Q3 growth of 11.4%, against an assumed 8%): in 2026 the business repeatedly outran careful bottom-up models. I would raise 2027 organic growth toward 5.5% and the margin toward 7.0% on a Q4 print above 8% with the backlog still above 3.2 months. I would cut toward the bear path if copper fell below $12,000/t or European volume turned negative.

Conclusion: a credible path of about 12% EPS growth a year to 2030, a margin about 100bp above the last cycle's average and nearly double the cash flow, with the operating line above consensus and the 2027 EPS line below it for non-operating reasons.

Score: 78, set by the Rater. About 12% sits in the 10-15% B band; I place it a little above mid-band because the margin averages about 7.0% over 2027-30 against about 6.0% over 2019-25 and reaches a past peak without inflation, but held there because organic growth after 2027 is only 3-4%, about a third of the margin step is bought (GCG), and dilution and interest keep per-share growth below group earnings growth.

#7 Scope for upgrades to guidance, estimates and the narrative over 6-12 months

Guidance. Guidance is far more likely to be raised than cut over the next twelve months, and three scheduled events can move it: 10 February 2027 (FY2026 results, the first FY2027 outlook, GCG closed with a first PPA estimate, and the dividend), late April (Q1 sales and GCG's first quarter) and late July (H1 results).

Guidance is far more likely to be raised than cut over the next twelve months.

Viewforth's probabilities. The red segment for FY2026 is a miss (10%).

A raise of FY2027 guidance would most likely come in July 2027, as in 2023 and 2026, and would be incremental. A cut would most likely come in October 2027, when the +11.4% comparison makes "confirm" the likely tone of the Q3 release. On the mid-term framework, the margin above 7% is more likely to arrive early, in 2028, than late. A new capital-markets-day framework with 2030 targets is more likely than not within 18 months (I expect a margin of 7.5% or more and North America above 55% of sales), and it would read as a raise.

Consensus. The key call is the split along the income statement: consensus operating estimates should rise, while consensus EPS is held. Consensus revenue, EBITDA and EBITA for 2026-28 should be upgraded over six months, by 3-5% for 2026 EBITA and 4-8% for 2027 EBITA, in two steps.

  • The Q3 beat. Morgan Stanley has already raised its 2027 EPS by 2.7%, Bernstein has raised its 2027 margin to 7.2%, and Jefferies expects "mid-single-digit upgrades to consensus EBITA".
  • GCG's consolidation. After closing, the nine brokers that exclude GCG will add about €1,050m of revenue and about €120m of EBITA.

Consensus 2027 EPS is more likely to be held within ±3% of €3.00 than upgraded in step, because four below-the-line items offset the operating upgrade: the surcharge extension (-3%), the full post-placing share count (-1% to -5%), GCG's interest cost and, for brokers that do not add it back, PPA (-6%).

The French budget process has firmed the base case and narrowed the tail risk. The National Assembly's Finance Committee adopted the one-year surcharge extension on 13 October. On 4 November the Assembly rejected the entire revenue section of the bill (section 458-0), which sends the government's original text, extension included, to the Senate from 20 November and makes passage by Article 49.3 or by ordinance plausible. Either route implements the government's draft, so the extension stays in Viewforth's base case. The rejection also deleted the committee's amendments, which most likely removes the proposals that Morgan Stanley flagged on 28 October to enlarge the surcharge by up to 30 points on French revenue above €3bn.

The February 2027 headline will pair an operating beat with an EPS reset for tax, share count and PPA that most of consensus has not modelled.

Narrative. The narrative can only improve from today's frame. Investors today frame Rexel as "a French construction cyclical with a leverage, dilution and placing overhang and an indirect exposure to AI". The frame this memo supports is "self-help plus a North American specialty mix shift, delivering volume-led growth with a record backlog and a margin floor 200bp above past troughs". The chain below sets out, in order, the five steps that move the market from the first frame to the second.

The developments of months six to eighteen are not in the current narrative at all. Several favourable dynamics are known to almost nobody: the countercyclical FCF, the breadth of the Q3 volume recovery and the convergence of data-centre margins toward regional levels. One unfavourable dynamic is also known to few: the mix of EPS bases inside consensus.

Where I differ from the market. The dashboard's sell-side momentum grade of A will not simply continue. I expect EBITDA revisions to stay positive and EPS revisions to turn mixed in February, a case in which the composite signal masks its components. The market expects more of the same; I expect an upgrade cycle led by the operating line, with a pause in EPS that the shares, down 12% on the placing, have partly discounted.

Counter-case and what would change my view. If most contributors already add PPA back (Jefferies says nine do), the gap between consensus EPS and Viewforth's EPS is only about 1%, and the February reset is smaller than I fear. If the surcharge lapses in the final December vote, 2027 consensus EPS is right and Viewforth's EPS rises 3%. Copper above $15,000/t through H1 2027 would add 4-5% to consensus EPS; copper at $11,000/t would cut it 8-10%.

Conclusion: good scope for operating upgrades to guidance and estimates over the next twelve months, a narrative that can only improve from "French cyclical", and an EPS line that pauses for policy and basis reasons in February before it resumes.

Score: 63, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, is more likely raised than cut: FY2026 beaten with about 75% odds and FY2027, about to be guided below the run-rate, raised about 50% against 15% cut, a raise worth roughly 0.5 times the 4.5% organic growth rate; operating consensus should rise 3-8% as the Q3 beat and GCG are absorbed, and the narrative has room to improve from 'French cyclical'. Held below the 75 level because the line that drives the price, 2027 EPS, is more likely held or reset 3-8% lower in February for tax, share count and PPA than upgraded, consistent with the fourth-set group (60).

#8 Current momentum: guidance, estimates, narrative, technicals, and peers

Guidance and estimates. Operating momentum is strong: guidance has been raised twice in a year, and consensus for FY2027 is rising across the income statement (chart below). The mean target price has risen 12% over six months to €41.91, 28% above the share price; the share of Buy ratings is 71%, up 29 points in six months; and the dashboard grades sell-side momentum A, with a revision-momentum score of 15, the highest of the 13 stocks in its sector.

EBITDA and sales revisions have outrun EPS revisions by three to four points, which is the effect of dilution and interest. Part of the sales and EBITDA revisions also reflects copper and GCG's consolidation by four brokers rather than organic improvement. The A grade is therefore genuine at the operating line and overstated at the EPS line.

Share price and technicals. Price momentum is weak: the dashboard grades technical momentum D. The price is 8.4% below a 200-day average that has risen in each of the last twelve months, and below the 50- and 150-day averages; the relative-strength percentile is 39; and the shares are down 8% over three months and 1.6% over six months, against +14.7% over twelve. The shares fell 11.8% in the three months after the GCG announcement and placing, while 2027 EPS estimates rose 4%. The €34.75 placing price is now technical resistance, as participants in the placing sell near their entry price.

The shares have decoupled from their peers: over six months Rexel fell while the distributor basket rose, and the link between them has largely broken.

Narrative. The narrative is adverse. Markets are risk-off, with defensive stocks leading; Viewforth's regime digests rate Rexel Double Underweight on both Fragility and Country (France); the electrical and climate wholesaler cohort is the only falling group in its sector; and the French sovereign spread is at a fifteen-year high. Thematic fit and momentum are rated C, on the environment only.

Peers are re-rating without Rexel. Most of the sector has B-grade technical momentum (over twelve months: Bossard +52%, Bufab +39%, RS Group +34%, Brenntag +28%); Indutrade and RS Group have A, and only Rexel, Addtech, Diploma and Lagercrantz have D. Wesco is up about 50% year to date, against 13% for Rexel. Rexel's P/E of 11.0x is the lowest in the sector (range 12.6-27.5x), yet at the 82nd percentile of its own history Rexel is as expensive against itself as Bossard, Bufab and Diploma, whose valuation grades are F.

Inference. Sell-side momentum of A beside technical momentum of D is the signature of owners selling into upgrades. The de-rating is happening through the denominator: the two-year-forward P/E has fallen from 13.0x in February to 11.0x with the share price roughly unchanged, so earnings are outrunning the de-rating. That pattern is uncomfortable to hold, and in the sector's history it is the condition under which cheap, geared distributors later outperform when the market regime turns.

Where I differ from the market. The market treats the decoupling as a verdict on the business; I read it as a verdict on the listing (France), the funding (the placing) and the theme (AI). The French and placing concerns resolve on known dates; the AI concern has no date.

Counter-case and what would change my view. Because 84% of the share's variance is idiosyncratic, a sector rally lifts Rexel less (beta 0.78), and each results release and each French political date carries event risk. A close back above the €34.75 placing price and the 200-day average on the February results would mark the technical turn. A share sale by Cevian would remove the takeover floor and replace it with an overhang.

Conclusion: strong and real operating momentum in guidance and estimates, weak price momentum and an adverse narrative, and peers re-rating without Rexel: the gap between the two is the opportunity and the discomfort.

Score: 60, set by the Rater. One measure strongly positive and one negative gives C. Guidance raised twice, 2027 EPS up 4% over three months and 7% over six (79th-80th percentile, about 0.9 times the revenue growth rate) and buy ratings up 29 points lift it into the upper half of the band, while the price below its 50-, 150- and 200-day averages, an adverse France and placing narrative and peers re-rating without Rexel keep it from moving a letter.

#9 Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and expectations

Simplicity. The case is simple to state (price and copper, data centres, GCG, self-help), and its 2027 drivers are few, dated and observable. By 10 February 2027 the market will know the readings on three of the four drivers (GCG's closing and parameters; the copper price against $13,700/t; the backlog and data-centre share), as well as the text of the Finance Bill. Rexel's disclosure lets each driver be tested within one reporting cycle. The disclosure gaps are no quarterly margin (so the price-over-cost spread is visible only twice a year), no GCG segment data until February at the earliest, and no UK or German country margins.

Fragilities and requirements. The forecasts require five conditions to hold, and they do not require four others.

The forecasts require

  • Copper near $13,700/t: every $1,000/t is 1 point of growth and 10-15bp of margin
  • Hyperscaler capex that keeps converting a backlog in which data centres are a quarter
  • GCG closing by year-end and running at about an 11% margin
  • Non-cable price near +1.7%, against opex inflation of 2.6%
  • Core volume growing about 1.5 points in H2 2027, against the hardest comparison since 2022

The forecasts do not require

  • A European construction recovery before 2028
  • A buyback
  • A tax cut
  • A bid

The 2027 range of outcomes is skewed down on EPS and flat on cash (diagram below). The most likely form of a miss is a zero reading for core volume in H2 2027, which would arrive with the Q3 release in October 2027, outside the window in which guidance can protect the shares.

The 2027 cone is skewed down on EPS and flat on cash: free cash flow is €700-780m and leverage below 2.3x in every scenario.

Suddenness, predictability, prevalence and materiality of share-price risks. The share-price risks are more sudden than the earnings risks, and they fall into three groups.

Kind of riskThe risks
Sudden and sentiment-drivenAn AI-capex or neocloud credit scare that hits the whole data-centre basket; a blow-out in the French spread (the June 2024 snap election widened the spread 29bp in a week and took Rexel down 7.6%, and the current episode is wider and longer); read-across from Wesco's data-centre growth or from Fastenal's and Graybar's gross margins (Graybar's fell 50bp to 18.9% in Q3 on competitive pricing); a copper sell-off; Cevian selling.

Bounded tailsThe €48m judicial guarantee; a UK exit; an outage of the enterprise resource planning (ERP) system or a cyber attack.

Sector and cyclicality precedents. Distributors move with factory orders, one to two quarters behind. In a restock with inflation, distributors "win three ways" for 6-18 months, and Rexel is 12-18 months into this window. In deflation with volume declines, distributors give back 70-100bp of margin on low-single-digit organic declines (2012, 2015, 2020, 2024). The multiple falls ahead of the earnings: Rexel's two-year-forward P/E fell to 6.5x in mid-2022 while margins were at a record.

A plausible bad case takes the shares to about €24-25 (-25%), through either a de-rating to the 10th-percentile multiple of 7.3x on intact earnings or a 15% earnings cut at the 35th-percentile multiple of 8.6x. A severe compound case (recession plus copper deflation) takes the shares to €18-20. Below about €28, the level of QXO's rejected bid, private-market interest provides a soft floor in a non-recessionary setting; on the other side of that floor, Bernstein's view is that any serious bid would have to start above €40.

Where I differ from the market. The market frames the risk as "a European construction cyclical with leverage". The real fragility is a correlated AI-and-copper reversal, and the real cushion, countercyclical FCF with leverage below 2.3x in every scenario against a 3.5x covenant, is barely discussed. The leverage and dilution that the market worries about are the least risky parts of the case.

Counter-case and what would change my view. The earlier research sets shared a conservatism (every one under-called the Q3 run-rate), which argues for a fatter upside tail than the text implies; for that reason I weight the bull case at 25%, against 20% for the bear case. Each reading in the "breaks" column of the monitor below would move me toward the bear case.

#10 Where the stock is in its lifecycle

The dashboard's reading is Bottoming. The dashboard's rule weights the price and technical readings: the price is below all moving averages, relative strength is in the bottom half, sell-side momentum is high, and the valuation grade is F (the current P/E is at the 82nd percentile of ten years).

My reading: two clocks are running, and the diagram below sets out the evidence for each. On fundamentals, the stock is in the reinforcing phase and the thesis is broadening. On price, the stock turned up from a trough in late 2023, peaked in February 2026 and has stalled for nine months on a sequence of company-specific overhangs: the Q1 miss and French spreads (February-April), the cooling of the AI trade, and then the GCG placing and buyback pause (September-October). The stock is now bottoming in price while reinforcing in fundamentals.

Richard's framework assigns lower multiples to turning-up and stalling phases, because forecasts in those phases are more uncertain, and higher multiples to phases of peak delivery. Rexel's forecasts are unusually certain for the next eight months and uncertain for H2 2027; the delivery is of peak quality, but the environment is not.

Two clocks: the fundamentals are reinforcing while the share price is bottoming after a nine-month stall on dated overhangs.

  • 3.4-month backlog

  • estimates rising for twelve months; buy ratings up 29 points
  • a step-change acquisition aimed at the diagnosed weakness

  • February 2026 peak: 13.0x, €35.7

  • overhangs: Q1 miss and French spreads, AI trade cooling, GCG placing and buyback pause

Which phase for valuation purposes. For valuation, Rexel is between turning up and reinforcing, with the price lagging the fundamentals by two to three quarters. The same lag occurred in 2018-19, when Morgan Stanley noted that "the market failed to credit the turnaround" at 7.7x EV/EBITA, before the re-rating of 2021-22. The overhangs that caused the stall resolve on dates: placing absorption (now), the French budget (December), GCG's closing (year-end) and the February results. The AI-capex question does not resolve on a date, and it is the one overhang that could turn "bottoming" into "collapsing".

Where I differ from the market. The dashboard rule says Bottoming; the bulls say reinforcing and under-valued; the Sell says stalling, with the self-help in the price. I am closest to the dashboard on the price clock and to the bulls on the fundamental clock, and the gap between the two clocks is the investment case.

I side with the dashboard on the price clock and with the bulls on the fundamental clock; the gap between them is the case.

Counter-case and what would change my view. If the February results beat and the shares still cannot recover the €34.75 level, the market is saying that the overhang is the AI theme or France rather than the placing, and the phase is a longer stall. If H2 2027 organic growth falls toward 2% with copper rolling over, the fundamental clock joins the price clock in stalling.

Conclusion: bottoming in price after a nine-month stall, reinforcing in fundamentals; the two clocks should converge between February and July 2027 if the dated overhangs clear.

But it is not Broadening: Rexel is 12-18 months into the restock-with-inflation window, the inputs peak in rate of change into 2027 and H2 2027 faces the hardest comparison since 2022, so mid Reinforcing with a lagging price.

#11 The fair multiple

The guideline. The dashboard's starting phase is Bottoming, and its guideline fair multiple is 8.38x two-year-forward earnings: the 30th percentile of Rexel's own ten-year history, and 24% below today's 11.0x. The model applies the guideline to its own forward EPS, on which today's multiple is 10.2x, so the model assumes a de-rating of about 18-19% by December 2027.

Ten-year bandPercentileTwo-year-forward P/E

What the history says the market pays. The ten-year history of Rexel's multiple is a lesson in anticipation (eras below): the market pays a high multiple when earnings are depressed and about to recover, and a low multiple when earnings are peaking and about to fall. In H2 2022, for example, the multiple fell to 6.5-7.6x while margins were at a record 7.3%, because the market was pricing the deflation that followed. By that pattern, today's 11.0x says that the market still treats 2026-27 earnings as a recovery rather than a peak. The question for the multiple is whether 2027-28 reads as a peak (copper, data centres) or as mid-cycle (self-help, GCG, and a European recovery still ahead).

Rexel's multiple is high when earnings are depressed and about to recover, and low when they peak.

My fair multiple over 18 months is the median of 9.3x as the central case, with 8.4x as the bad-case anchor and 10.5x as the bull case. Three lines of reasoning support that view.

  • Against the guideline's level. 8.38x is a trough-phase multiple, and Rexel is not in a trough. Rexel is delivering and raising guidance; its trough margin is 200bp higher than in earlier cycles; North America and specialties move above half of sales with GCG; the FCF yield at today's price is 7-9% for 2027-28; and the shares have already de-rated by two turns while peers re-rated. The peer-relative evidence argues that some of the discount is temporary: a 38% discount to capital goods, against 25% historically; a 30% discount to Wesco, against 15%; and Legrand, with the same 19% French exposure, on 15.3x EV/EBITA. So do the deleveraging precedents: Wesco re-rated from about 7x to about 12x forward EV/EBITDA as its leverage fell after the Anixter acquisition, and Beijer Ref re-rated within twelve months of the rights issue for its Heritage acquisition.
  • Against a return to 12x or more. On Rexel's own history, a two-year-forward P/E above 11x has occurred only at points of trough earnings. Rexel is a BB+-rated, French-listed, copper-exposed cyclical distributor with an unhedged dollar exposure, a 6-7% margin borrowed from suppliers' pricing power, returns on acquired capital near the cost of capital and asymmetric operating leverage. The 2027 EPS range is skewed down, and rising discount rates compress compounders and cheap stocks alike. The sell-side's mean target of €41.91 implies about 12x Viewforth's 2028 EPS, which I would not underwrite.
  • The path matters. Overhangs that are non-fundamental and mostly dated are setting the multiple today. If the February results beat and the French budget passes without enlargement, the "prudent" median is reachable by mid-2027; if copper and the AI trade turn together, the "crash" band of 7.3x is the plausible bad case, as in 2022.

Where I differ from the market and from the guideline. The guideline is too harsh on the level of the multiple and right on its direction. A de-rating from 11x toward the median is my base case too, because earnings growth of 12% a year will outrun a flat price, and because 2027-28 carry more peak-like risk than 2026. The bulls' 12x is too generous for Rexel's balance sheet, listing and cyclicality.

Counter-case and what would change my view. A bid (from QXO, from CVC or through a process sponsored by Cevian) would bypass the public multiple: Bernstein's threshold of €40 or more is 23% above the price and would make the multiple debate moot. A credible 2030 framework with a margin above 7.5% and resumed buybacks would justify the 75th-percentile multiple (10.5x); a Cevian exit or an enlarged French tax would justify the 35th (8.6x).

Conclusion: the guideline's 8.38x is the right anchor for the bad case but a trough multiple for a delivering company; my fair multiple over 18 months is the ten-year median of 9.3x, with 7.3x and 10.5x as the tails.

Score: 54, set by the Rater. Dear on one measure and cheap on the other gives C. I place it in the lower part of the band because part of the peer cheapness is deserved (BB+ balance sheet, French listing, borrowed margin, Wesco's higher data-centre exposure) and the memo's own fair multiple, the 9.3x median, sits below today's 10.2-11.0x, while the high own-history percentile is somewhat flattered by a multiple that only exceeded 11x at trough-earnings points.

#12 Total shareholder return: the DuPont split

At the guideline multiple, the model's total return is small over 18 months and modest over three years.

What drives the guideline return, step by step.

  1. Today the shares trade on 10.2x the model's two-year-forward EPS of about €3.20.
  2. By December 2027, two-year-forward earnings are FY2029's €3.70 (+16%). At the assumed 8.38x, the price is €31.0 (8.38 × €3.70), below today's €32.63, and the €1.20 and €1.35 dividends (+€2.55, or +7.8%) carry the total return to +2.9%.
  3. By June 2029, forward earnings are about €4.15 (+30%), the price at 8.38x is €34.8, and three dividends (€4.05) take the total value to €38.81 (+18.9%).

In short, earnings growth contributes about 18% over 18 months and 39% over three years; the guideline multiple takes back all of the first and most of the second; and the dividends are the steady part, growing from €1.20 to €1.75 (a yield on today's price rising from 3.7% to 5.4%, at a payout of about 47%).

What is certain, and what is not. The earnings leg to 2027 is the most predictable part of the case: FY2026 is about 90% known, and H1 2027 is backed by the backlog and the arithmetic of GCG's consolidation. The FY2029 EPS of €3.70 that sets the 18-month forward earnings requires a 7.15% margin and about 3.3% organic growth, both plausible and both unproven. The dividend leg is high-confidence: FCF covers the dividend two to three times, the policy floor is a 40% payout, and a flat FY2026 dividend at €1.20 is already in the model. The multiple leg is the swing factor.

Layering the EPS range on top widens the outcomes. The bear EPS path (2027 €2.42; FY2029 about €3.25) at 7.3x gives about €23.7 plus €2.55 of dividends, a total return of about -20%. The bull path (2027 €3.36; FY2029 about €4.10) at 10.5x gives about €43 plus €2.55, a total return of about +40%. The probability-weighted 18-month return at my central multiple of 9.3x, on the model's base earnings, is about +13%; at the guideline it is +3%; and the sell-side's +28% needs about 12x.

Where I differ from the model and the market. The model's +3% says that the multiple compresses to a trough level while the earnings compound. That return is internally consistent and the right anchor for the bad case, but as a central case it conflicts with the delivery, the peer discount and the deleveraging precedents. My central 18-month return is about +13%, roughly 8-9% a year, made of about +16% from earnings, about -9% from a de-rating to the median and about +8% from dividends; over three years my central return is about +31%, or 9-10% a year. The sell-side's 28% in twelve months assumes no de-rating and a lapse of the tax surcharge, and I would not lean on either assumption.

One turn of multiple = about €3.70 a share = 11% of the price
The one-turn difference between the guideline's 8.38x and the median's 9.3x is the decision Richard is being asked to make.

Counter-case and what would change my view. Two developments would make the guideline's return the right one: a reversal of copper and AI capex in 2027, which would take FY2029 EPS toward €3.25 and the multiple toward 7.3x at once, and an enlarged French tax with a disorderly budget. Two developments would make the bull return plausible: a July 2027 raise with GCG at a margin of 11% or more, and a confirmed buyback restart for 2028.

Conclusion: at the guideline multiple the shares return about 3% over 18 months and 19% over three years because a 19-23% de-rating cancels 18-39% of earnings growth; at the ten-year median the same earnings give about 13% and 31%, and that one-turn difference in the multiple is the decision Richard is being asked to make.

Score: 55, set by the Rater. About +13% sits in the C band and maps to about 57; I move it down two points for the fat, correlated lower tail (+3% at the guideline multiple, -9% at the 7.3x crash multiple and about -20% on the bear EPS path), with the three-year check of about 9-10% a year preventing a lower placing.

#13 Summary conclusion on the business and the investment case

Rexel is a well-managed, cash-generative, thin-margin distributor at the point in its cycle where delivery is strongest and the share price is weakest.

For: the next three results releases are more likely to raise expectations than to cut them. FY2026 will beat a twice-raised guide, the FY2027 guide will be set below what the business is already doing, and operating consensus will be upgraded as brokers absorb the Q3 beat and GCG. Earnings compound at about 12% a year to 2030 on drivers that are few, dated and trackable, and FCF nearly doubles while leverage returns below 2x in every scenario except the bear case.

Against: about half of 2026's growth was price, the inputs are at their peak rate of change, H2 2027 faces the hardest comparison since 2022, operating leverage is three to four times steeper on the way down, and the three growth drivers are correlated through the AI-and-electrification trade. The February 2027 headline will pair an operating beat with an EPS reset for tax, share count and PPA that the market has not modelled.

The return turns on the multiple. The shares are cheap against peers and dear against their own history. At the guideline multiple the model's return is close to nil over 18 months and modest over three years. The case for a better return rests on the multiple settling at the ten-year median rather than at a trough level; the dated overhangs (the placing, the French budget, GCG's closing) make that plausible by mid-2027, and the undated one (the financing of AI capex) could deny it.

The decision is therefore less about whether Rexel delivers, which it probably will, than about whether the market pays a median multiple for a delivering French cyclical in a risk-off, France-averse regime. The signposts that will settle the question are dated and few.

Five signposts, dated and few, decide the case.

Foundations' Robustness: 57, set by the Rater. A business of median quality (52) is lifted by a delivery record that is a reliable floor (76), a 200bp higher trough margin, countercyclical cash flow and near-duopoly European cores; it stays well short of Richard's stability-led 75s because margins are borrowed from suppliers, returns on new capital sit near the cost of capital and EPS still swings 25-35% across a cycle.

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 55, set by the Rater. The case straddles a Demand-driven EPS Upgrader (data centres, copper, electrification) and a Big Corporate Change-driven EPS Upgrader (GCG, self-help, mix) without fitting either cleanly: the demand leg is half price and peaking in rate of change, and the corporate leg is a moderate, partly bought step-up with dilution and leverage as present frictions; the high own-history multiple is left to topics 11 and 12.

Case Riskiness: 50, set by the Rater. Over Riskiness and simplicity (50): conservative guidance, few trackable drivers and a robust cash and balance-sheet floor make the operating case simple, but a down-skewed EPS cone, correlated AI-and-copper drivers, asymmetric operating leverage and sudden French and thematic share-price risk on a multiple high in its own range make it a typical rather than a low-risk case.

End notes

1. Bases of measurement. EPS on the memo's own figures is on the model's basis: recurring, before amortisation of acquired intangibles (purchase price allocation, PPA), after the French tax surcharge, on basic shares. To reach the after-PPA basis on which FactSet's FY2025 actual (€2.19) and most of consensus sit, deduct about €0.11 in 2026 and about €0.20 from 2027. Margins are Rexel's "current adjusted EBITA" margin. Leverage is on the company's definition (net financial debt excluding leases, over EBITDA after leases, EBITDAaL) unless stated. Consensus estimates are shown by named financial year.

2. Terms. Same-day sales growth is organic growth adjusted for the number of working days. Delta inflation is selling-price inflation less opex inflation. White space is the data hall of a data centre, as distinct from its power and utility infrastructure. Two-year-forward P/E is the price over earnings two financial years ahead.

3. Free cash flow in 2027. The model deducts GCG's roughly €150m of acquired working capital a second time in 2027, although that working capital is already paid for inside the €1,624m acquisition line. 2027 equity FCF should therefore be read as about €775m. The Financial Analyst should exclude acquired balances from the working-capital change rather than distort the working-capital ratio.

4. Sources. Visuals marked "drawn for this page" and the charts in visuals/drawn and visuals/drawn-copy-editor take their figures from the memo's text. Default visuals come from FactSet, the Master Dashboard and the one-page summary of the Financial Analyst's model of record (update 2); their notes give the basis. Richard's five financial tables (annual history, recent periods, FactSet consensus, broker detail and segments) are FactSet data.

5. Ratings. The four case ratings are given with their scores; on the page's grade scale, the Thesis's Change Forces' Strength score of 68 is a C (B is 75 to 89).

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
